title: Gildongmu
pitch: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Gildongmu means "traveling companion" in Korean. I started it in June 2026 to fix a small, stubborn problem of my own as a screen reader user: I wanted to look up an address and call a place as fast as possible. Map apps make both slow, because their answers live in an interface built around images. So Gildongmu has no map at all. Everything it knows, it says in words: places, routes, what is around you, and the accessibility details a screen reader user actually needs, such as station elevators, audio beacons, accessible restrooms, stairs-free walking routes and crosswalks with audible signals. Almost all of that comes from Korean public data. When I read about WebMCP, I realized that this had quietly prepared the app for agents. Every sentence a screen reader user hears is a sentence an agent can be handed. This entry is what happened when I handed them over. What it does Gildongmu is a free navigation app for South Korea with no account and no ads, on the web, on iOS, and as an npm command line tool and MCP server. It joins about thirty public and commercial APIs from nineteen organizations and turns them into plain text. As far as I know, it is the first navigation app in Korea where a screen reader user can search places, plan a trip and explore the surroundings with no barrier in between. For this challenge the web app declares seven WebMCP tools to the browser agent: describe_app: what this deployment can do and how the tools chain search_places: places, addresses and web results, with refs to pass on get_place_info: a place by ref; for stations the timetable, accessibility facilities, live arrivals and barrier-free facilities plan_directions: transit, walking and driving summaries for a destination get_transit_route_detail: one transit route in full, including the boarding door for a quick exit get_route_steps: walking or driving steps as a numbered page read_current_view: which screen the app is on and what it shows Ask the agent "Tell me the first train, the last train and the elevators at Gangdong Station (강동역)" and one tool call brings all of it back. Ask "Seoul Station (서울역) to Gangnam Station (강남역): which car and door should I board to get off next to the elevator?" and while the agent answers, the app in the browser tab has already moved to that route, so the user can turn on VoiceOver and check every line. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The answers were already text. Most navigation apps keep their answer in pixels, so an agent driving a browser has to guess at a canvas. Gildongmu had to write every answer as a sentence for VoiceOver users long before it ever met an agent. Those same sentences are what the tools return, and they come from the same code that draws the screen. The agent cannot be told something the screen does not say. Neither a plain browser agent nor a server MCP can do this alone. Behind one station answer are four public APIs, each with its own key, its own response format and, in Korea, its own coordinate system. An agent reading the page cannot rebuild that. A server MCP, on the other hand, cannot answer "where am I standing right now", because it has no browser tab. WebMCP sits exactly in between: the page keeps the keys and the location, and the agent asks in words. Location stays in the browser. A trip starts from the user's current position, which the page already knows. Tool output goes through a list of allowed fields that has no place for coordinates, so the agent's provider receives place names and sentences, never a coordinate pair. Gildongmu has promised since its first release that nothing personal is stored on its servers, and the tools keep that promise. How it creates a better user experience For a screen reader user the expensive part is not reaching a screen, it is exploring it. A transit plan on screen is dozens of items, one swipe at a time. As a tool result it is one spoken answer, and the app has still moved to that same screen, so the user can take over and verify anything. The size of an answer follows the same instinct. A full transit answer came out at 3,700 characters, far past the 1,500 the guidance recommends. Instead of cutting it off, I split it the way I would say it out loud: the recommended route in full, the other routes in one line each, and the details behind a second tool. Nothing got worse for people. The tools press the same functions a person clicks, and a person always wins. Type a new search or close a section while a tool is running and the tool call ends as superseded. If a dialog is open, the tool declines instead of closing it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before "Which car and door do I board so that I get off next to the elevator?" Gildongmu matches a public quick exit dataset to the live route, so get_transit_route_detail returns the boarding door for each leg. No map tells you this. Ask it in the chat, and the app is already sitting on that route. "Does Gangdong Station have an elevator, and when is the first train?" One call to get_place_info returns the timetable, the accessibility facilities, the real time arrivals and the barrier-free facilities. Without WebMCP the agent would open four sections one by one, and it could not call the four public APIs behind them at all. The handoff goes both ways. The agent and the user share one screen: the tools move the app, and read_current_view reads whatever the person did by hand. The agent can set up a trip that the user finishes by touch, or the user can search by hand and then ask the agent about what is on the screen. Before this, asking an assistant and using an app were two separate places that did not know about each other. Honest absence. Every tool tells apart "none", "not known" and "lookup failed", and says outOfCoverage outside Korea instead of inventing a result. A screen reader user cannot glance at a screen to catch a made up answer, so the tools never let the agent guess. The app has followed the same rule for people since version 1.0. How I implemented WebMCP I used the imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool with a name, a description, an input schema and an execute function. Here is how I understand what I built: One set of seven tools, registered once at the app root, because an agent reads the tool list once. A tool that is not configured on this deployment is still declared and answers notConfigured. A tool that needs another screen moves there itself. Each screen publishes a small bridge to a registry, and a tool reads it at the moment it runs. A tool that waits for a screen waits for a specific place id or sequence number, not for a screen name, so a call about place A cannot be satisfied by place B appearing first. Onl

Hi, I'm Hunyong Kim. As a blind person, I built Gildongmu, a text-based navigation app for South Korea. Every answer is text, not a map. For a screen reader user, a transit plan is dozens of items, one swipe at a time. Here is what WebMCP changes. The page registers seven tools: search, place info, trip planning, route
details, and reading the screen. The agent now knows the tools and how they
connect. Without WebMCP, the agent would search, open
the station page, and read four sections one by one: timetable, facilities, elevators, live
arrivals. Behind them are four public APIs the agent
cannot call itself. With WebMCP, one tool call returns all of
it. First train, last train, elevator, in one
answer. And every sentence comes from the same code
that draws the screen. A full transit answer is 3,700 characters. The limit is 1,500. So the tool gives the best route in full,
other routes in one line, and details on request. No map tells you this: which car and door put the user next to the
elevator. And the output never contains coordinates. The app is now on the route screen the agent
described. The user can turn on a screen reader and
check every line. The tools move the app, and the agent reads
what the user does by hand. They share one screen. I have been building Gildongmu
for about three months. The seven WebMCP tools, though, were built during the submission period, in about 30 commits, with over 100 tests. The code is open under MIT. Thank you.

live_observation.first_impression: A text-first English navigation interface presents a place search, voice search, Directions and Nearby controls, with location currently unavailable.
live_observation.action_attempted: Entered “Seoul Station” in the place search and clicked Search.
live_observation.after_state: The app displayed 21 places with category filters and accessible button descriptions containing names, categories, and addresses.
live_observation.notes: The no-map, plain-text search workflow worked and returned structured place results.
